To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) MAML is primarily effective because it reuses features, and (2) ANIL is a simple and effective algorithm that is a simplification of the MAML algorithm, and (3) ANIL is effective because it learns features that generalize well across tasks.

MAML's performance is primarily due to feature reuse (not to primed learning), that ANIL (which removes the inner loop for the network body) is an effective meta-learning algorithm that matches MAML's results, that ANIL's performance is entirely due to the learned representations, and that the NIL algorithm, which removes the inner loop even for the head of the neural network, can match ANIL's performance.

(1) feature reuse is the main factor for MAML's performance and (2) we can achieve MAML's performance without any inner loop, and with a computational cost that is only slightly higher than that of the original MAML algorithm.

the meta-initialization in MAML is not primed for fast learning, but is primed for fast adaptation to new tasks by leveraging the features that it has already learned, which is why it works well in the first place.
